name: The Three Holy Hierarchs
description: Sts. Basil the Great, Gregory the Theologian, and John Chrysostom — the three great hierarchs and ecumenical teachers, each individually venerated yet jointly commemorated.

name: Synaxis of the Holy Twelve Apostles
description: The Twelve whom Christ chose and sent to preach the Gospel to all nations, commemorated together as a synaxis on the day after Sts. Peter and Paul, alongside their individual feasts.

name: The Seventy Apostles
description: The Seventy whom Christ sent out two by two (Luke 10), commemorated together as a synaxis alongside their individual feasts.

name: Synaxis of the New Martyrs and Confessors of Russia
description: Those who suffered for Christ during the Soviet-era persecutions of the twentieth century, commemorated together as a synaxis.

name: Synaxis of the Holy Myrrh-bearing Women
description: The women who came to the tomb of Christ bearing myrrh to anoint his body and first received news of the Resurrection, honored together with the Most Holy Theotokos, who is numbered first among them, and with the two secret disciples Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus, who took the Lord's body from the Cross. Commemorated on the Sunday of the Myrrh-bearers, the third Sunday of Pascha.

name: The Holy Chief Apostles Peter and Paul
description: The two chief apostles — Peter the fisherman who confessed Christ and Paul the apostle to the nations — each individually venerated yet jointly commemorated as the pillars of the Church.

name: The Holy and Righteous Ancestors of God, Joachim and Anna
description: The parents of the Most Holy Theotokos and grandparents of the Lord according to the flesh, commemorated together on the day after the Nativity of the Theotokos.

name: The Sunday after Nativity: Joseph the Betrothed, David the King, and James the Brother of the Lord
description: Joseph the Betrothed, the Prophet-King David, and James the Brother of the Lord, jointly commemorated on the Sunday after the Nativity of Christ.

name: Synaxis of the Optina Elders
description: The startsy of Optina Monastery — from Leonid and Macarius through Ambrose and Nectarius — who renewed eldership in nineteenth-century Russia, commemorated together as a synaxis.

name: Martyrs of Nicomedia with Hieromartyr Anthimus
description: Bishop Anthimus of Nicomedia and the martyrs who suffered with him in the Diocletianic persecution at Nicomedia, commemorated together on September 3.

name: Synaxis of the Two Theodores
description: The soldier-martyrs Theodore the Recruit and Theodore Stratelates, paired throughout Orthodox hymnography and iconography as the Two Theodores.

name: The Seven Deacons
description: The seven men of good repute chosen by the apostles to serve the early Church (Acts 6), headed by the Protomartyr Stephen and including Philip the Evangelist.

name: The Holy Family of Cappadocia
description: The remarkable saintly household of fourth-century Cappadocia — Basil the Great with his grandmother, parents, sister, and brothers — among the most numerous families of saints in the Church.

name: Saint Mary of Egypt and Saint Zosimas
description: The penitent Mary of Egypt and the hieromonk Zosimas who found her in the desert and gave her Communion, commemorated together on the Fifth Sunday of Great Lent.

name: Holy Patriarchs of Alexandria, Athanasius and Cyril
description: The two great Alexandrian patriarchs and defenders of Orthodox doctrine, Athanasius the Great and Cyril of Alexandria, jointly commemorated on January 18.

name: The Family of the Forerunner
description: The household of Saint John the Baptist — his father the priest Zechariah and his mother Elizabeth, kinswoman of the Theotokos.

name: Equals-to-the-Apostles Constantine and Helen
description: The first Christian emperor and his mother, who found the True Cross — jointly commemorated as the Equals-to-the-Apostles who gave the Church peace.

name: The Holy Prophet Moses with Aaron and Miriam
description: The prophet Moses with his brother Aaron the High Priest and his sister Miriam the prophetess — the kin who led Israel out of Egypt.

name: Saints Cosmas and Damian with their Mother Theodota
description: The holy unmercenary twin physicians of Asia and their devout mother Theodota, who raised them in the faith and is commemorated with them.

name: Synaxis of All Saints of North America
description: The saints glorified in North America — from the Alaskan missionaries and native faithful to the confessors, hierarchs, and new martyrs of the New World.

name: Synaxis of All Saints of Mount Athos
description: The saints of the Holy Mountain of Athos — its founders, hesychasts, wonderworkers, and new martyrs, gathered from the monastic republic.

name: Synaxis of the Saints of Britain and Ireland
description: The saints of the British Isles from the age of the undivided Church — Celtic and Anglo-Saxon monastics, missionaries, bishops, and martyrs.

name: Synaxis of the Saints of Alaska
description: The saints of Alaska — the missionaries, martyrs, and native faithful who planted and watered the Orthodox faith in the far north.

name: The Household of Bethany — Lazarus, Martha, and Mary
description: Lazarus the Four-Days-Dead, whom Christ raised, with his sisters Martha and Mary — the household of Bethany that the Lord loved and often visited.

name: Synaxis of the Holy Unmercenaries
description: The Anargyroi ("without silver") — the physician- and healer-saints who took no payment for their care, headed by Cosmas and Damian and the Great Martyr Panteleimon. An open synaxis: each is commemorated on his own day, and all are honored together on October 17 in Greek practice and on the Sunday after November 1 in Slavic practice.

name: Synaxis of the Holy Forefathers and Foremothers
description: The whole company of the righteous of the Old Covenant — the forefathers from Adam, the patriarchs and matriarchs, the judges, the kings and the prophets — commemorated together on the Sunday of the Holy Forefathers, two Sundays before the Nativity of Christ. An open synaxis: every saint of the Old Testament era belongs to it, and each keeps his own day besides.

name: The Thirteen Syrian (Assyrian) Fathers of Georgia
description: The thirteen ascetics who came from Syria to Georgia in the sixth century under John of Zedazeni and planted monasticism across the kingdom, founding the houses of Zedazeni, Shio-Mgvime, Davit-Gareji, Alaverdi and Nekresi. Commemorated together on May 7, and several of them again on their own days.

name: The Confessors of Transylvania
description: The Romanian priests, monks and laymen of eighteenth-century Transylvania who refused the union with Rome and suffered imprisonment and death for the Orthodox faith, commemorated together on October 21.

name: The House of Nemanjić
description: The founding dynasty of Serbian sanctity — Stefan Nemanja, who ended his reign as the monk Symeon on Athos, his wife Anastasia and his son Sava, and the kings, queens and archbishops of four generations after them. Few royal houses have given the Church so many saints.

name: The Holy Fathers Slain at Sinai and Raithu
description: The ascetic fathers of Mount Sinai and of Raithu on the Red Sea, cut down by raiders while at prayer in their cells — two massacres, remembered by the Church on one day with the survivors who wrote down what they saw.

name: Synaxis of the Hierarchs of Novgorod
description: The bishops, archbishops and metropolitans who shepherded the see of Novgorod the Great from Joachim of Korsun onward, most of them buried in the Cathedral of Holy Wisdom, whose common commemoration began when Saint John appeared to Archbishop Euthymius II in 1439 and bade him serve a panikhida for them.

name: Synaxis of the Moscow Hierarchs
description: The metropolitans and patriarchs of Moscow honoured together — Peter, Alexis, Jonah, Philip and Hermogenes, the five of the ancient commemoration, with Job, Innocent, Macarius and Tikhon added as the Church glorified them.

name: Synaxis of the Hierarchs of Perm
description: Stephen, apostle of the Zyrians, who gave them an alphabet and the Scriptures in their own tongue, with the bishops who followed him in that missionary see and were killed for it.

name: Synaxis of the Serbian Hierarchs
description: The archbishops and patriarchs of the Serbian Church from Saint Sava onward, commemorated together on August 30 — the succession of Žiča and Peć through independence, empire and Ottoman rule.

name: The Serbian New Martyrs of the Second World War
description: The bishops, priests and lay faithful of the Serbian Church killed in the persecution of 1941–45 in the Independent State of Croatia, among them the martyrs of the Jasenovac camp, whose collective commemoration is kept on August 31.

name: The Holy Despots — the Household of Branković
description: The blinded despot Stephen, his wife Angelina who carried his relics through exile, and their sons John and Maximus — a family that lost a country and was glorified for what it kept.

name: The Confessors of Ardeal
description: The Romanian hierarchs and priests of seventeenth-century Transylvania who suffered imprisonment, deposition and death rather than give up the Orthodox faith under Calvinist and Habsburg pressure, commemorated together on April 24. Distinct from the eighteenth-century Confessors of Transylvania kept on October 21.

name: The Three Athonite New Martyrs
description: Euthymius, Ignatius and Acacius, three monks of the Holy Mountain who went out under Ottoman rule to confess Christ before the Turks and were beheaded within two years of one another; their relics were gathered to the Skete of Saint Anna and they are commemorated together on May 1.

name: The Martyrs of Najran
description: Arethas, elder of the city of Najran in southern Arabia, with the great company killed with him in 523 by the Himyarite king Dhu Nuwas for refusing to deny Christ — the noblewoman Syncletica and her daughters among them — and the Ethiopian king Elesbaan, who broke the persecutor's power and ended his life a recluse.

name: The Fathers of the Dalmatos Monastery
description: Isaac, who withstood the Arian emperor Valens to his face, and Dalmatus and Faustus who followed him as abbots of the monastery at Constantinople that took Dalmatus's name — three generations of one house, commemorated together on August 3.

name: Synaxis of the Saints of Kazan
description: The saints of the Kazan land — the first hierarchs Gurias, Barsanuphius and Herman sent to a newly-conquered khanate, the martyrs Peter and Stephen killed by their own neighbours for baptism, and Hermogenes, who found the Kazan icon there and died a patriarch's death in Moscow.

name: Saints Theonas, Symeon and Phorbinus of Egypt
description: Three fathers of the Egyptian desert whose names the calendar has kept together on April 5 though little else of them survives — a commemoration that stands for the whole unnumbered company of the Egyptian solitaries.

name: Synaxis of the Venerable Fathers of the Kiev Near Caves
description: The monks, iconographers, chroniclers, physicians and wonderworkers whose relics rest in the Near (Anthony) Caves of the Kiev Caves Lavra, commemorated together on September 28 besides their own days.

name: Synaxis of the Venerable Fathers of the Kiev Far Caves
description: The fathers whose relics rest in the Far (Theodosius) Caves of the Kiev Caves Lavra — recluses, fasters, canonarchs and schemamonks — commemorated together on August 28 besides their own days.

name: Synaxis of the Glinsk Elders
description: The elders of the Glinsk Hermitage, masters of the prayer of the heart whose rule was drawn from Athos and Paisius Velichkovsky, and whose eldership survived two closures of the monastery and the Soviet camps.
